extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate and graduate students learning how to do academic research
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for finding, evaluating, and engaging scholarly and other sources for class papers, theses, and research projects, including how to ask librarians/experts, search catalogs and databases, evaluate relevance and reliability, and use sources ethically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare clear, rehearsed questions before asking librarians or experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare your questions and, if necessary, rehearse them before consulting a reference librarian or expert; describe your project using a concise three-step rubric (what I'm working on, what I want to find out, why I care).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give a short project statement such as: 'I am working on X to find out Y because I want to Z. Can you help me find…?' If shy, e-mail librarians. Specialists exist in large libraries. The quality of help depends on the quality of your questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use teachers and advanced students as expert resources but be specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask your teacher or advanced students to help focus your topic and suggest sources, but don't assume they have all answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rehearse questions before consulting; expect different levels of involvement (daily advising vs independent work) and choose a balance that suits your project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult general reference works early
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with general reference works (e.g., Encyclopaedia Britannica) to find basic sources and bibliographical leads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you find nothing under one heading, try related headings (the example: 'gender' might appear under 'sex' in older directories). Check end-of-article references in general references for leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult specialized reference works and online bibliographic databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Look up your topic in specialized encyclopedias or dictionaries and consult the references cited there; use library online bibliographical databases which often include abstracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In new or highly specialized fields use scholar/department/association web pages cautiously (they can be less reliable but useful to start). Many databases include abstracts and sometimes full text (often for a fee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use annotated bibliographies and annual review journals to survey a field
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek out annotated bibliographies and journals that review new research to efficiently learn what other researchers consider important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chronicle of Higher Education and 'books received' lists in journals can help find the newest books. Many fields publish yearly review journals that summarize new work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search the library catalog by keywords and by browsing subject headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Start keyword searches with the specific terms used to narrow your topic; once you find books, check Library of Congress subject headings and use them to find related titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for subject headings on a book's title page or its catalog 'details' page. Use the browse link to view books with similar call numbers to discover related works beyond keyword matches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit overabundant search results by date and use interlibrary options
rubrics_metrics.description: If a catalog search yields too many titles, narrow results by publication date (last 15 years, then last 10) or other filters; use interlibrary loan or buy books too new for your library.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large catalogs may show far more than your library holds; your library can usually borrow items. For books too new to be cataloged, check online booksellers or your library's new acquisitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use online journal databases for article-heavy topics
rubrics_metrics.description: If most sources are journal articles (especially in social sciences), search library online journal databases directly, using abstracts to decide which articles merit careful reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Databases let you search titles and keywords; browsing is less common there. For very current information, consult periodical indexes and online newspaper archives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Browse the stacks physically for serendipity
rubrics_metrics.description: Physically browsing library stacks can reveal unexpected, valuable sources you would miss online; scan shelves near promising books, check bindings, tables of contents, indexes, and bibliographies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scan titles on the shelf above, below, and beside target books and skim nearby journals' bound volumes (last ten years). Be suspicious of books lacking an index or bibliography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Internet mainly for primary sources and verify reliability for secondary use
rubrics_metrics.description: The Internet is valuable for primary materials (e.g., fan blogs as primary sources), library resources, government reports, and some scholarly journals, but is less trustworthy as a secondary or tertiary source unless you can demonstrate reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The web lacks gatekeepers; a site's popularity doesn't equal accuracy. Use internet sources freely when they are primary; otherwise show why a specific site is reliable before citing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect authors' copyright and prefer authorized copies
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid citing unauthorized electronic copies of recent texts; when a recent text is posted without clear author permission, use the print edition instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unauthorized e-versions often reproduce texts inaccurately and may violate the law; cite database or authorized postings when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate sources on two main axes: relevance and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have many potential sources, screen them quickly using relevance (does it address your question?) and reliability (is it a trustworthy source?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fast skimming techniques to assess relevance (see separate relevance checklist). Use the reliability checklist (publisher reputation, peer review, author credentials, sponsorship, currency, notes/bibliography, web bibliographic data, judicious tone, reviews, citation frequency) to judge trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skim books, articles, and websites efficiently to judge relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: For books: skim the index for keywords, prologues, introductions, summaries, and chapter first/last paragraphs, and check bibliographies. For articles: read abstracts, skim introductions and conclusions, section headings, and bibliographies. For websites: treat like a printed article when possible and look for 'About', 'Site Map', or a site search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speedy reading methods guide both research and writing: if your report isn't structured so readers can skim it, it has a problem. For collections, read the editor's introduction; for journals, check tables of contents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete indicators to evaluate reliability (publisher, peer review, author, sponsorship, currency, notes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the source is published by a reputable press, whether it was peer-reviewed, whether the author is a reputable scholar, whether an online source is sponsored by a reputable organization, whether the source is current for your field, and whether books and sites provide notes and bibliographical data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific checklist items from the text: 1) reputable press (university presses generally reliable), 2) peer review status, 3) author credentials and possible conflicts of interest, 4) site sponsorship and maintenance/updating, 5) currency appropriate to the field (computer science vs humanities), 6) presence of notes/bibliography, 7) websites listing bibliographic data, 8) judicious tone and absence of advocacy/abuse/errors. For advanced students also consider: 9) whether the book has been well reviewed and 10) how often it has been cited (citation index). These indicators do not guarantee reliability; always read critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow bibliographical trails
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a source's bibliography and works-cited to find earlier and related work; authors cited most often in an index are often important in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal articles typically review prior research at the start — follow those citations. One source leads to others and creates a trail that helps navigate difficult research territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look beyond predictable sources to enrich research
rubrics_metrics.description: Especially for advanced projects (MA/PhD), search outside the standard reference types for relevant material (e.g., plays, prints, economic history) to enrich analysis and build originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't ignore relevant works not cited in bibliographies: finding a useful overlooked source can earn credit for originality. Use diverse materials to synthesize different kinds of data.

rubrics_metrics.name: When prior work appears to solve your question, reformulate or improve
rubrics_metrics.description: If you find a source that seems to pose and solve your exact problem, either formulate a new question or find ways to do better than that source (e.g., correct errors, extend, or refine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't panic; the published question rarely matches yours exactly. Consider whether you can improve on the source's method, evidence, or interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use people as primary sources ethically and prepare interviews carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: When collecting data from people, plan what you want to know, prepare questions without scripting rigidly, and consult your institution's Human Subjects Committee/IRB to ensure you 'do no harm.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interview planning increases efficiency; avoid aimless questioning. Institutional review is required for research involving people to protect them from embarrassment or privacy violations; follow committee guidance even if it feels bureaucratic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record complete bibliographical data before reading a source
rubrics_metrics.description: Before reading a source, record full bibliographic details so you can credit sources accurately and recover them later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For books: author, title, editors/translators, edition, volume, place published, publisher, date, page numbers consulted. For journals: author, article title, journal title, volume/issue, date, page numbers. For online: include URL, date accessed, webmaster (if any), and database name. When photocopying, copy the title page and publication data; if you access a printed text online, cite original printing details as well as access info.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage sources actively: read generously first, then critically, and verify claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Read important sources at least twice: first generously to understand, then slowly and critically to evaluate arguments; summarize passages mentally before disagreeing and check accuracy of important claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't accept claims solely because an authority asserts them. Beware of confirmation bias (favoring evidence that supports your claim). Advanced researchers should check accuracy of everything central to their argument and consult primary sources where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know what kinds of evidence fields expect
rubrics_metrics.description: Different disciplines expect different evidence types: personal anecdotes (first-year writing), direct quotations (humanities), verbal descriptions (history), fine-grained recorded artifacts (anthropology), and quantitative experimental/survey data (social and natural sciences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present data in the forms your readers expect; avoid using inappropriate formats (e.g., bar charts for literary development). If unsure what's sufficient or representative in your field, ask a teacher or expert and request examples of failed arguments caused by inadequate evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use secondary sources for both data and ideas but verify and assess sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Use secondary sources to supply data, models, and claims, but verify important material in primary sources when possible and judge whether evidence is sufficient and representative for your field and the stakes involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't accept secondary-reporting of quotations without checking originals. Statistical claims require judgment about how data were collected/analyzed; different fields require different sample sizes and standards of representativeness. Ask experts for examples of insufficient evidence in your field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use secondary sources to generate research problems via creative agreement or disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Find research problems by either extending/confirming useful claims (creative agreement) or by identifying contradictions and limitations (creative disagreement) in existing work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative agreement examples: offer additional or stronger evidence, confirm unsupported claims, or apply a claim more widely. Creative disagreement types include contradictions of kind, part-whole contradictions, developmental/historical contradictions, external cause-effect contradictions, and perspective-based contradictions; each can point to new research questions and approaches.
